S Sathyanarayana Rao INTRODUCTION Depression is a common disorder, which often leads to poor quality of life and impaired role functioning. It is known to be a major contributor to the global burden of diseases and according to World Health Organization (WHO), depression is the fourth leading cause of disability worldwide and it is projected that by 2020, it will be the second most common leading cause of disability. Depression is also associated with high rates of suicidal behaviour and mortality. When depression occurs in the context of medical morbidity, it is associated with increased health care cost, longer duration of hospitalization, poor cooperation in treatment, poor treatment compliance and high rates of morbidity. Depression is also known to be associated with difficulties in role transitions (e.g., low education, high teen child-bearing, marital disruption, unstable employment) and poor role functioning (e.g., low marital quality, low work performance, low earnings). It is also reported to be a risk factor for the onset and persistence of a wide range of secondary disorders. Available data also suggests that between one-third and one-half of patients also experience recurrence of depressive episodes. ASSESSMENT AND EVALUATION (table-1) Table 1. Components of assessment and evaluation Management of depression involves comprehensive assessment and proper establishment of diagnosis. The assessment must be based on detailed history, physical examination and mental state examinations. History must be obtained from all sources, especially the family. The diagnosis must be recorded as per the current diagnostic criteria. Depression often presents with a combination of symptoms of depressed mood, loss of interest or pleasure, decreased energy and fatigue, reduced concentration and attention, reduced self-esteem and self-confidence, ideas of guilt and unworthiness, bleak and pessimistic views of the future, ideas or acts of self-harm or suicide, disturbed sleep and diminished appetite. Depending on the severity of depression some of these symptoms may be more marked and develop characteristic features that are widely regarded as having special clinical significance. These symptoms are known as somatic symptoms of depression and include symptoms of loss of interest or pleasure in activities that are normally enjoyable, lack of emotional reactivity to normally pleasurable surroundings and events, waking up in the morning 2 hours or more before the usual time, depression worse in the morning, objective evidence of definite psychomotor retardation or agitation (remarked on or reported by other people), marked loss of appetite, weight loss (often defined as 5% or more of body weight in the past month) and marked loss of libido. It is important to note that for the diagnosis of depressive disorder these symptoms need to be present for at least 2 weeks and need to be associated with psychosocial dysfunction. Some of the patients with depression may present with predominant complaints of aches, pains and fatigue and they may not report sadness of mood on their own. A careful evaluation of these patients often reveals the underlying features of depression. However, it is important to note that many patients with depression will also have associated anxiety symptoms. With increasing severity of depression patients may report psychotic symptoms and may also present with catatonic features. Thorough assessment also ought to focus on evaluation for comorbid substance abuse/dependence. Careful history of substance intake need to be taken to evaluate the relationship of depression with substance intoxication, withdrawal and abstinence. Whenever required appropriate tests like, urine or blood screens (with prior consent) may be used to confirm the existence of comorbid substance abuse/dependence. Many physical illnesses are known to have high rates of depression. In some situations the physical illnesses have causative role in development of depression, whereas in other situations the relationship/co-occurrence is due to common etiology. When depression occurs in relation to physical illness attempt may be made to clearly delineate the symptoms of depression and physical illness. Further, while making the diagnosis, it maybe clearly mentioned as to which diagnostic approach [i.e., inclusive approach (symptoms are counted whether or not they might be attributable to physical illness), substitute approach (nonsomatic symptoms are substituted with somatic symptoms), exclusive approach (somatic symptoms are deleted from the diagnostic criteria) or best estimate approach] was followed. fetched_contents.text: Deprescribing INTRODUCTION — Deprescribing is an essential part of good prescribing and is inherently linked to related activities, such as medication reconciliation, to ensure safe and effective use of medications. This process requires attention, time, and in many cases special skills and knowledge. This includes technical knowledge, such as optimal down-titration schedules, as well as competencies in shared decision making, communication, and managing health systems in a medical culture that historically has been more oriented toward adding medications than stopping them. A more general discussion of drug prescribing in older adults is provided separately. (See "Drug prescribing for older adults".) Deprescribing is most commonly employed in older adults, people with multiple chronic conditions, and people near the end of life. However, deprescribing can be appropriate in any patient taking medication. (See 'Which patients and which medications should be targets for deprescribing?' below.) This topic will provide information on approaches to deprescribing, including common barriers and how to address them. Related issues regarding discontinuing antihypertensive and antidepressant agents are discussed in detail elsewhere. (See "Tapering and discontinuing antihypertensive medications" and "Antidepressant discontinuation syndrome and discontinuing antidepressants in adults".) DEFINITION — The term "deprescribing" refers to a process of medication withdrawal, supervised by a health care professional, with the goal of managing polypharmacy and improving outcomes [1]. This can encompass efforts to comprehensively review a patient's medication list and systematically discontinue or reduce the dose of all medications with an unfavorable balance of benefits and harms, as well as efforts focused on specific types of high-risk medication. What distinguishes deprescribing from traditional approaches to pharmaceutical care is that it encourages a systematic and proactive approach. Deprescribing focuses on being proactive to address medication-related problems that have not previously been identified or satisfactorily managed and to prevent future problems. GOALS OF DEPRESCRIBING — The overall goal of deprescribing is to improve patient important outcomes. Patients can vary in their experience of potential benefits and harms from medication use, how they value these outcomes, and their attitudes toward medication withdrawal. Therefore, the goals of deprescribing can vary between patients. For example, for a patient who has recently suffered an injurious fall, deprescribing efforts may focus on reducing use of medications that confer increased fall risk. In another patient who is troubled by taking multiple medications dosed multiple times per day, efforts may focus on reducing medication regimen complexity and burden. Common goals for deprescribing include reducing overall medication burden, reducing the risk of specific geriatric syndromes such as falls and cognitive impairment, and improving global health outcomes such as hospitalization and death. Ultimately, all these goals relate to improving quality of life. Specific goals can include: ●Reducing medication burden – Overall, deprescribing interventions are generally effective in reducing the number of medications and improving appropriateness of medication use [2]. Careful medication review and aggressive discontinuation can lead to reduction in up to 39 percent of medications used [3], including reducing use of potentially inappropriate medications by up to 30 to 60 percent or more [4-6]. Reducing medication burden may improve adherence to remaining medications [7]. ●Reducing risk of falls – Many medications increase fall risk among older adults, including benzodiazepines and benzodiazepine receptor agonists (eg, zolpidem and zopiclone), antidepressants, antipsychotics, and strongly anticholinergic medications [8-11]. In nursing home settings, deprescribing programs using broad-based medication review have been shown to reduce fall risk by 24 percent [4]. Efforts to reduce use of psychotropic medications have also reduced the rate of falls, albeit with highly variable results across studies [12,13]. However, while deprescribing of fall-risk increasing drugs and other potentially inappropriate medications appears clinically sensible, several studies have found that interventions to deprescribe these medications have not meaningfully affected the rate of falls [2,6,14-16]. (See "Falls: Prevention in community-dwelling older persons", section on 'Medication modification' and "Falls in older persons: Risk factors and patient evaluation", section on 'Medication use' and "Falls: Prevention in nursing care facilities and the hospital setting", section on 'Medication use'.) ●Improving and/or preserving cognitive function – Anticholinergic medications, sedative-hypnotics including benzodiazepines and benzodiazepine receptor agonists, and use of multiple psychotropic medications can negatively affect cognition [9]. However, several studies have found no meaningful improvement in cognitive function in people with and without dementia following a deprescribing intervention [17,18]. By contrast, a small number of studies have found a benefit when deprescribing psychotropic medications [19-21]. ●Reduce risk of hospitalization and death – Overall, there are mixed findings on the impact of deprescribing interventions on hospitalization and death [2,22]. In vulnerable older adults residing in nursing homes, trials of interventions incorporating whole-regimen review and deprescribing reduced hospitalization by 36 percent and death by 26 percent [4]. In ambulatory settings, a systematic review found that interventions using whole-medication review had no impact on hospitalization but did reduce mortality by 26 percent [6], although methodologic challenges may reduce confidence in this finding [2,22,23]. fetched_contents.text: Comparing efficacy of telehealth to in-person mental health care in intensive-treatment-seeking adults Abstract The heightened acuity in anxiety and depressive symptoms catalyzed by the COVID-19 pandemic presents an urgent need for effective, feasible alternatives to in-person mental health treatment. While tele-mental healthcare has been investigated for practicability and accessibility, its efficacy as a successful mode for delivering high-quality, high-intensity treatment remains unclear. This study compares the clinical outcomes of a matched sample of patients in a private, nation-wide behavioral health treatment system who received in-person, intensive psychological treatment prior to the COVID-19 pandemic (N = 1,192) to the outcomes of a distinctive group of patients who received telehealth treatment during the pandemic (N = 1,192). Outcomes are measured with respect to depressive symptoms (Quick Inventory of Depressive Symptomatology-Self-Report; QIDS-SR) and quality of life (Quality of Life Enjoyment and Satisfaction Questionnaire; Q-LES-Q). There were no significant differences in admission score on either assessment comparing in-person and telehealth groups. Patients in the partial hospitalization level of care stayed longer when treatment was remote. Results suggest telehealth as a viable care alternative with no significant differences between in-person and telehealth groups in depressive symptom reduction, and significant increases in self-reported quality of life across both groups. Future research is needed to replicate these findings in other healthcare organizations in other geographical locations and diverse patient populations. Keywords: Behavioral health, Mental health, Telehealth, COVID-19 1. Introduction In response to the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic, healthcare organizations around the world adapted to remote behavioral health treatment to meet an increased need for high-quality mental health care. With lockdowns and stay-at-home orders, the pandemic presented an acute need for mental health treatment to be virtually accessible—regardless of patient or provider setting—as well as near-equivalent in quality to what a person would have received had they attended in person. This paper examines the current landscape of remote mental health care as a viable treatment delivery method and uses clinical outcomes data from patients undergoing in-person and telehealth mental health treatment at a large, multistate behavioral health system to illustrate telehealth's comparability to traditional, in-person care. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reported that symptoms of anxiety and depressive disorders among adults “increased considerably” when comparing reports from April through June of 2019 to the same time period in 2020 (Czeisler et al., 2020). In the survey with 5,412 adult respondents, the CDC measured anxiety and depressive symptoms related to the pandemic using the four-item patient health questionnaire (PHQ-4) and COVID-19 trauma-related symptoms using the six-item Impact of Event Scale. Overall, 40.9% of survey respondents reported at least one adverse mental health condition, including symptoms of anxiety disorder or depressive disorder (30.9%), and 26.3% reported symptoms of a trauma- and stressor-related disorder because of the pandemic. Suicidal ideation in the last 30 days was reported by 10.7% of respondents. In 2021, the CDC published results of the Household Pulse Survey, a self-report online survey, which showed that the percentage of adults who reported experiencing symptoms related to depression and anxiety disorders increased from 36.4% to 41.5% between August 2020 and February 2021 (Vahratian et al., 2021). Additionally, respondents who reported unmet mental health needs increased from 9.2% to 11.7% in the same time period. Historically there is evidence that mental health needs increase during a pandemic (Soklaridis et al., 2020). Past outbreaks, such as severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) in 2003, directly resulted in heightened anxiety related to the virus (Cheng and Cheung 2005; Chong et al., 2004), as well as increased stigmatization and discrimination of minority groups (Ren et al., 2020). Feelings of uncertainty, isolation, and confusion over rapidly changing health guidelines have exacerbated feelings of anxiety and mental distress (Rajkumar, 2020). What sets the COVID-19 pandemic apart is the already widespread use of telecommunication platforms for remote work, learning, and basic healthcare. Although prior studies have investigated the impact of telehealth compared to traditional in-person treatment, there has been limited research into these differences in treatment settings beyond the outpatient level (Hilty et al., 2013). This is a novel offering of the current analysis. Mental healthcare providers have been exploring remote treatment options for over six decades (Hilty et al., 2013). In this domain, providers use videoconferencing for therapy, evaluations, and medication management. In some cases, clinicians use telehealth to supplement in-person treatment. Previous research has shown that telehealth reduces patient-incurred costs and time associated with travel (Rabinowitz et al., 2010) and improves accessibility of mental healthcare for those living in rural areas (Manfredi et al., 2005; Morland et al., 2010; Weiner et al., 2011). Some even argue that remote treatment is superior to in-person consultations for some patients (Pakyurek et al., 2010; Storch et al., 2011). In the context of public health, others have highlighted telehealth as a way for patients to maintain human connection during social distancing and lockdowns (Whaibeh et al., 2020). How to make the next telehealth appointment as helpful as possible

A telehealth appointment can be very helpful if the patient comes prepared, communicates clearly, and asks for concrete next steps. The evidence supports using telehealth as a viable care alternative with no significant differences in depressive symptom reduction between in-person and telehealth groups, and it suggests that telehealth may be appropriate for follow-ups and medication management [N2-R1][N2-R3]. However, it also implies that telehealth is not a perfect substitute for every type of evaluation and that some care may still require in-person interaction [N4-R5][N4-R4].

What to prepare ahead of time for the appointment  
The best preparation is to bring any relevant changes in symptoms, mood, energy, sleep, appetite, or daily functioning. The evidence on how to talk to a doctor about depression recommends clearly explaining symptoms and being honest and thorough about how you feel emotionally and physically [N5-R5]. That same advice also emphasizes asking questions and preparing in advance to get the most out of the visit [N5-R1]. For a telehealth follow-up, patients should also note any side effects from medication, any new stressors or life changes, and any barriers to attending appointments [N5-R4]. If the patient has a telehealth provider, they should also confirm the format of the visit and whether they will need to share any lab results, medication list, or other documentation in advance.

How to ask for clear next steps and refill instructions  
The evidence supports asking the provider directly for clear next steps and refill instructions. One source explicitly says that follow-ups for medication management can last 15 minutes and that the provider will give guidance after the initial visit [N2-R5]. Another source emphasizes that talking to a provider should include asking questions and preparing in advance [N5-R1]. A practical approach is to state, “I need clear instructions on when to refill, whether I should adjust my dose, and what to do if I run out.” This aligns with the guidance that patients should be honest and thorough when describing their symptoms and ask for help sorting them out [N5-R3].

When to request a follow-up sooner than the scheduled date  
The evidence on telehealth triage says that delays in mental health care can worsen symptoms, increase safety risks, and make recovery more difficult [N4-R3]. It also states that in-person care is necessary when symptoms create safety risks, involve rapid behavioral changes, or include physical symptoms that need medical attention [N4-R1]. In that context, if the patient feels their depression is worsening, they should ask the provider to reschedule sooner than planned. The evidence also suggests that providers assess appropriateness of in-person versus telehealth based on diagnosis and symptoms [N4-R4]. So if the patient is experiencing something that feels urgent, such as increased suicidal thoughts, more severe low mood, or changes that make daily life harder, they should request a follow-up earlier [N4-R1][N4-R3].

Bottom line  
To make the next telehealth appointment as helpful as possible, prepare by bringing symptom changes and any questions you want to ask; ask for clear next steps and refill instructions; and request a sooner follow-up if symptoms feel worse or more dangerous than usual [N2-R1][N2-R5][N4-R1][N4-R3][N5-R1][N5-R5].

Limits and risks of relying on telehealth once a month

Telehealth can be useful, but it has clear limits when used infrequently, especially for major depression. The evidence says telehealth is a viable care alternative with no significant differences in depressive symptom reduction between in-person and telehealth groups, but it also highlights that telehealth may not capture everything that an in-person evaluation can [N2-R1][N4-R4]. For major depression, this matters because evaluations often depend on observing behavior, mood, and physical symptoms that may not be fully visible over a short video call [N4-R1]. The evidence also notes that providers assess the appropriateness of in-person versus telehealth based on diagnosis and symptoms [N4-R4], which means that some patients may need more frequent or in-person contact.

What telehealth may miss in a major depression evaluation  
The evidence does not give a direct checklist of what telehealth misses, but it does imply that some aspects of care may be harder to assess remotely. One source says telehealth may be appropriate for follow-ups and medication management, but it does not say it is equally effective for every part of a depression evaluation [N2-R3]. Another source says delays in mental health care can worsen symptoms and increase safety risks, which suggests that infrequent follow-up may miss early warning signs [N4-R3]. The evidence on telehealth triage also states that in-person care is necessary when symptoms create safety risks, involve rapid behavioral changes, or include physical symptoms that need medical attention [N4-R1]. That means telehealth may miss subtle but important changes in mood, behavior, or physical health that could signal a worsening episode.

When in-person care is better or safer  
In-person care is better or safer when the patient’s depression is severe, when there are safety risks, rapid behavioral changes, or when physical symptoms require medical attention [N4-R1]. The evidence also says that in-person visits will be required within 6 months prior to an initial telehealth visit and every 12 months thereafter under Medicare telehealth rules [N4-R5]. That rule underscores the importance of in-person contact for ongoing care, especially when the provider wants to maintain continuity and ensure safety. If the patient is on a medication that requires regular monitoring or if symptoms are fluctuating, in-person care is likely the safer option [N4-R1][N4-R5].

How to advocate for more frequent contact if needed  
If the patient feels their care is not sufficient, the evidence supports asking the provider directly about more frequent contact. The guidance on talking to a doctor recommends preparing questions and being honest about symptoms [N5-R1][N5-R5]. The evidence on telehealth triage also supports requesting a sooner follow-up if delays could be dangerous [N4-R3]. So the patient should say something like, “I’m worried about how often we’re meeting. Can we see each other more often, or can we arrange a quicker check-in if needed?” That approach is consistent with the evidence that providers should assess appropriateness of in-person versus telehealth based on diagnosis and symptoms [N4-R4].

Bottom line  
Telehealth can be helpful, but it may miss important signs of worsening depression, especially safety risks, rapid changes, or physical symptoms. In-person care is better or safer when symptoms are severe, dangerous, or require medical attention [N4-R1][N4-R3]. If the patient needs more frequent contact, they should ask the provider directly and explain why they feel the current schedule is not enough [N4-R4][N5-R1][N5-R5].

Options for urgent care if medication access is not resolved quickly

If medication access is not resolved quickly, the patient should consider acute or emergency care only if symptoms are clearly worsening, dangerous, or life-threatening. The evidence on urgent care does not provide a prescriptive step-by-step, but it does support the idea that delays in mental health care can worsen symptoms and increase safety risks [N4-R3]. It also says in-person care is necessary when symptoms create safety risks, involve rapid behavioral changes, or include physical symptoms that need medical attention [N4-R1]. This means the patient should treat medication shortages as a potential red flag, especially if they are already on a medication that is important for stabilization.

When acute care or emergency care is appropriate  
Acute care is appropriate when the patient needs prompt attention but is not in immediate life-threatening danger. Emergency care is appropriate when there is an acute medical emergency, such as overdose, severe withdrawal, suicidal crisis, or other urgent physical symptoms that require immediate treatment [N4-R1]. For depression, the evidence suggests that delays can worsen symptoms and increase safety risks, so the patient should consider urgent care if they are feeling more unstable than usual, experiencing new safety concerns, or having symptoms that prevent them from functioning [N4-R3][N4-R1]. If the shortage is of a medication that is necessary for stabilization, even a delay of a few days may matter.

What to expect from urgent care versus emergency departments  
Urgent care centers typically provide prompt, non-life-threatening care and may have shorter wait times than emergency departments, but they may not have the same level of specialized mental health resources [N4-R3]. Emergency departments are for life-threatening emergencies and may provide immediate access to medications or psychiatric evaluation, but they can be crowded and may not prioritize mental health issues as quickly as needed [N4-R3]. The evidence on prescription refill rules also notes that emergency refill options may be available depending on the plan and the situation [N3-R1]. So the patient should be realistic about what each setting can offer and choose the one that best fits the urgency of their situation.

How to ask for medication access during urgent care  
The evidence supports asking for medication access directly, but it does not specify exactly how. One source says that telehealth can be used for medication management and that providers may give guidance after the initial visit [N2-R5]. Another source emphasizes that patients should be honest and thorough when describing symptoms and ask for help sorting them out [N5-R5]. In an urgent care setting, the patient should state clearly: “I need access to my medication as soon as possible because my supply is running out, and I’m worried about my symptoms.” They should also ask whether the provider can prescribe a refill, adjust the dose, or connect them with a pharmacist [N3-R1][N5-R1][N5-R5]. If the provider cannot refill immediately, the patient should ask about emergency alternatives and follow-up options.

Bottom line  
If medication access is not resolved quickly, the patient should consider urgent care for acute but not life-threatening concerns and emergency care for serious safety risks [N4-R1][N4-R3]. In urgent care or the emergency department, they should ask directly for medication access, refill options, and help sorting out any worsening symptoms [N3-R1][N5-R1][N5-R5]. If the situation is clearly urgent, they should also ask whether a provider can prescribe a refill or connect them with a pharmacist [N3-R1][N5-R5].

The evidence supports an early refill or dose adjustment if the patient is at risk of running out, especially if symptoms are worsening. The clinical guidelines on depression management say that tapering should be done over several weeks to few months and that such tapering may allow for the detection of emerging symptoms or recurrences [N1-R1]. UpToDate on deprescribing also notes that some guidance recommends a slower taper, especially for psychotropic medications, and that deprescribing is a supervised process with clear goals [N1-R2][N1-F2]. That means the patient should not assume that a medication shortage is a reason to stop or drastically reduce a medication on their own. Instead, they should contact the provider early if they are running low, especially if they are on a medication that is important for stabilization [N1-R1][N1-R5].

Whether to request an early refill or adjust dose before the next appointment  
The evidence supports requesting an early refill if the medication shortage is imminent and the patient is not yet at the next appointment. The prescription refill rules indicate that many plans allow early refills for non-controlled substances and that emergency refill options may be available [N3-R1]. The evidence also suggests that providers may be able to prescribe medication via videoconference or supplement in-person treatment [N2-R3]. Therefore, the safest approach is to call the provider early, before the medication runs out, and ask whether an early refill is possible. If the provider is unavailable, the patient should ask about emergency refill options and whether they can connect with a pharmacist or telehealth service [N3-R1][N3-R2][N6-R1].

What symptoms or changes signal an urgent need for action  
The evidence on telehealth triage says delays in mental health care can worsen symptoms, increase safety risks, and make recovery more difficult [N4-R3]. It also says in-person care is necessary when symptoms create safety risks, involve rapid behavioral changes, or include physical symptoms that need medical attention [N4-R1]. So the patient should treat the following as urgent signals: increased suicidal thoughts or self-harm ideas, more severe low mood, worsening sleep or appetite, physical symptoms that may require medical attention, or changes that make daily life harder [N4-R1][N4-R3]. If any of these happen, the patient should seek immediate help rather than waiting for the next appointment.

How to contact the provider if the next appointment is not soon enough  
The evidence supports contacting the provider directly if the next appointment is not soon enough. The guidance on talking to a doctor recommends preparing questions, being honest about symptoms, and asking for help sorting them out [N5-R1][N5-R5]. The evidence on telehealth triage also supports requesting a sooner follow-up if delays could be dangerous [N4-R3]. So the patient should call the provider as soon as they realize their medication is running low and ask for refill options, dose adjustments, or a quicker appointment. If the provider is not available, they should ask about urgent care options and whether they can get a refill through a pharmacist or emergency care [N3-R1][N4-R3][N5-R1][N5-R5].

Bottom line  
If meds are running low, the patient should request an early refill or ask about dose adjustment before the next appointment, not wait for the scheduled visit [N1-R1][N3-R1]. They should treat any worsening symptoms, safety risks, rapid behavioral changes, or physical symptoms as urgent and seek help immediately [N4-R1][N4-R3]. If the next appointment is not soon enough, they should contact the provider directly and ask for refill options, quicker follow-up, or emergency care as needed [N3-R1][N5-R1][N5-R5].

# What you should do now, and what to expect next

## 1) What to do now if your meds are running low

The evidence says that if your medication is running low and you’re at risk of running out, the safest first step is to request an early refill or ask about a dose adjustment before your next appointment [N1-R1][N3-R1]. This is especially important if your depression is not stable, because the guidelines for depression management recommend tapering medication over several weeks to few months and warn that tapering may reveal emerging symptoms or recurrences [N1-R1][N1-F2]. The same evidence also says that when a shortage happens, options may include keeping the same dose, changing the dose, switching medications, or using nonmedication options [N1-R5]. So the first thing you should do is **contact your provider as soon as you realize your supply is low**.

If your provider is unavailable, the evidence supports looking for emergency refill options, because many plans allow early refills for non-controlled substances and emergency refill rules may apply depending on the situation [N3-R1][N3-R2][N6-R1]. The evidence also says that providers may be able to prescribe medication via videoconference or supplement in-person treatment, which is relevant if telehealth is part of your care plan [N2-R3]. So your best bet is:

- Call your provider early if your meds are low.
- Ask whether an early refill is possible.
- Ask whether a dose adjustment could help you avoid running out.
- If the provider cannot refill immediately, ask about emergency refill options or whether they can connect you with a pharmacist.

## 2) When to treat this as urgent

The evidence on telehealth triage is clear: delays in mental health care can worsen symptoms, increase safety risks, and make recovery more difficult [N4-R3]. It also says in-person care is necessary when symptoms create safety risks, involve rapid behavioral changes, or include physical symptoms that need medical attention [N4-R1]. So if any of these happen, you should act quickly.

### Signs that something is urgent
If you experience any of these, do not wait for your next appointment:
- **Increased suicidal thoughts or self-harm ideas**
- **More severe low mood or emotional pain**
- **Worsening sleep or appetite**
- **Rapid changes in behavior, energy, or functioning**
- **Physical symptoms that need medical attention**
- **Changes that make daily life harder or more dangerous**

If any of these are true, the evidence supports seeking immediate help rather than waiting [N4-R1][N4-R3].

- **Ask whether you should adjust your dose before the next appointment.**
- **If symptoms are worsening or dangerous, ask for help immediately.**

### Before the next appointment
- **Prepare by bringing symptom changes, side effects, and any questions.**
- **Ask for clear next steps and refill instructions.**
- **Request a sooner follow-up if your symptoms feel worse or more dangerous.**

- **Ask directly for medication access, refill options, and help sorting out worsening symptoms.**

If you’re on a monthly telehealth schedule and your meds are running low, the best course of action is:
1. Call your provider as soon as you realize your supply is low.
2. Ask whether an early refill or dose adjustment is possible.
3. If symptoms are worsening or dangerous, seek immediate help rather than waiting for the next appointment.
4. Prepare carefully for the next telehealth visit so it is as helpful as possible.
5. If telehealth feels insufficient, ask the provider directly whether in-person care or more frequent contact is needed.

That same advice also emphasizes asking questions and preparing in advance to get the most out of the visit [N5-R1]. To make the next telehealth appointment as helpful as possible, prepare by bringing symptom changes and any questions you want to ask; ask for clear next steps and refill instructions; and request a sooner follow-up if symptoms feel worse or more dangerous than usual [N2-R1][N2-R5][N4-R1][N4-R3][N5-R1][N5-R5].

Another source says delays in mental health care can worsen symptoms and increase safety risks, which suggests that infrequent follow-up may miss early warning signs [N4-R3]. That rule underscores the importance of in-person contact for ongoing care, especially when the provider wants to maintain continuity and ensure safety. Telehealth can be helpful, but it may miss important signs of worsening depression, especially safety risks, rapid changes, or physical symptoms. If medication access is not resolved quickly, the patient should consider acute or emergency care only if symptoms are clearly worsening, dangerous, or life-threatening. Acute care is appropriate when the patient needs prompt attention but is not in immediate life-threatening danger. Emergency care is appropriate when there is an acute medical emergency, such as overdose, severe withdrawal, suicidal crisis, or other urgent physical symptoms that require immediate treatment [N4-R1]. For depression, the evidence suggests that delays can worsen symptoms and increase safety risks, so the patient should consider urgent care if they are feeling more unstable than usual, experiencing new safety concerns, or having symptoms that prevent them from functioning [N4-R3][N4-R1]. If the shortage is of a medication that is necessary for stabilization, even a delay of a few days may matter.

Urgent care centers typically provide prompt, non-life-threatening care and may have shorter wait times than emergency departments, but they may not have the same level of specialized mental health resources [N4-R3]. Emergency departments are for life-threatening emergencies and may provide immediate access to medications or psychiatric evaluation, but they can be crowded and may not prioritize mental health issues as quickly as needed [N4-R3]. - Ask whether an early refill is possible.
- Ask whether a dose adjustment could help you avoid running out.
- If the provider cannot refill immediately, ask about emergency refill options or whether they can connect you with a pharmacist.

## 2) When to treat this as urgent

The evidence on telehealth triage is clear: delays in mental health care can worsen symptoms, increase safety risks, and make recovery more difficult [N4-R3]. - **Increased suicidal thoughts or self-harm ideas**
- **More severe low mood or emotional pain**
- **Worsening sleep or appetite**
- **Rapid changes in behavior, energy, or functioning**
- **Physical symptoms that need medical attention**
- **Changes that make daily life harder or more dangerous**

If any of these are true, the evidence supports seeking immediate help rather than waiting [N4-R1][N4-R3].

2. Ask whether an early refill or dose adjustment is possible.

## 1) What to do now if your meds are running low

The evidence says that if your medication is running low and you’re at risk of running out, the safest first step is to request an early refill or ask about a dose adjustment before your next appointment [N1-R1][N3-R1]. If your provider is unavailable, the evidence supports looking for emergency refill options, because many plans allow early refills for non-controlled substances and emergency refill rules may apply depending on the situation [N3-R1][N3-R2][N6-R1]. The evidence also says that providers may be able to prescribe medication via videoconference or supplement in-person treatment, which is relevant if telehealth is part of your care plan [N2-R3]. So your best bet is:

- Call your provider early if your meds are low.
- Ask whether an early refill is possible.
- Ask whether a dose adjustment could help you avoid running out.
- If the provider cannot refill immediately, ask about emergency refill options or whether they can connect you with a pharmacist.

## 2) When to treat this as urgent

The evidence on telehealth triage is clear: delays in mental health care can worsen symptoms, increase safety risks, and make recovery more difficult [N4-R3]. It also says in-person care is necessary when symptoms create safety risks, involve rapid behavioral changes, or include physical symptoms that need medical attention [N4-R1]. So if any of these happen, you should act quickly.

### Signs that something is urgent
If you experience any of these, do not wait for your next appointment:
- **Increased suicidal thoughts or self-harm ideas**
- **More severe low mood or emotional pain**
- **Worsening sleep or appetite**
- **Rapid changes in behavior, energy, or functioning**
- **Physical symptoms that need medical attention**
- **Changes that make daily life harder or more dangerous**

If any of these are true, the evidence supports seeking immediate help rather than waiting [N4-R1][N4-R3].

That means preparation is especially important.

### What to prepare ahead of time
Bring any changes in your symptoms, mood, energy, sleep, appetite, or daily functioning. The evidence on talking to a doctor recommends clearly explaining symptoms and being honest and thorough when describing how you feel emotionally and physically [N5-R5].
